export interface AsiabillFieldData {
  merNo?: string //	【商户号】
  gatewayNo?: string //【网关接入号】
  orderNo?: string //【商户订单号】 在该订单号是成功/待处理/待确认的状态下,不允许再次抛送此订单号。
  orderCurrency?: string //【交易币种】详见【附录】交易币种(ISO 4217)https://www.asiabill.com/developers/347-cn.html#currency
  orderAmount?: string //【交易金额】应为小数点后2位小数。
  firstName?: string //【客人的名】 长度必须在2-100之间。否则不能交易。
  lastName?: string //【客人的姓】 长度必须在2-50之间。否则不能交易。
  email?: string //【客人的邮件】 长度必须在2-200之间。否则不能交易。
  phone?: string //	【客人的联系电话】 长度必须在2-50之间。否则不能交易。
  paymentMethod?: string //【支付方式】 支付方式代码请参考具体支付接口
  shipFirstName?: string //【收件人的名】
  shipLastName?: string //【收件人的姓】
  shipPhone?: string //【收件人的联系电话】
  shipCountry?: string //【收件人的国家】
  shipState?: string //【收件人的州】
  shipCity?: string //【收件人的城市】
  shipAddress?: string //【收件人的地址】
  shipZip?: string //【收件人的邮编】
  returnUrl?: string //【交易返回地址】Asiabill处理完请求后，自动跳转到请求参数中的returnUrl地址。
  callbackUrl?: string //【后台通知地址】当传了此值则异步通知使用该URL通知
  remark?: string //【备注】可作为扩展信息，提交什么就返回什么。
}
slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code defines a TypeScript interface specifying structured payment and shipping data fields, including URLs for transaction return and callback, facilitating typed data handling for payment processing without performing any runtime actions.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided code is a TypeScript interface definition that statically describes the shape of payment and shipping data objects. It contains no executable logic, no data collection, no network requests, and no runtime behavior. Unlike the known malicious patterns, which actively collect sensitive data from the DOM and exfiltrate it to attacker-controlled domains, this code only defines types for structured data handling. There are no suspicious API calls, no obfuscation, and no evidence of data exfiltration or manipulation. The presence of comments in Mandarin is consistent with legitimate documentation and does not imply malicious intent. Therefore, this code is benign and serves as a type contract for payment processing data.

matched_knowledge.source_package: SilkSpecter Phishing Kit (custom web application (JavaScript/HTML, SaaS platform: oemapps))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user submits the payment form, the code collects credit card and cardholder data from form fields and sends it via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code collects sensitive payment information (card number, expiry, CVV, cardholder name) from the DOM and transmits it to a domain not associated with any legitimate payment processor, indicating data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate e-commerce sites should only send payment data directly to trusted payment processors (e.g., Stripe, PayPal) using secure APIs, and never to arbitrary or attacker-controlled external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate payment forms may collect and send data to PCI-compliant payment gateways, but never to unknown or untrusted domains outside the brand's control.
key_indicators: JavaScript code with Mandarin comments embedded in an English-facing site
HTTPS POST request to a suspicious domain (api.northfaceblackfriday.shop) unrelated to the brand
Direct access to and collection of card data fields from the DOM
No client-side validation or encryption before exfiltration

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user interaction on phishing site, specifically when payment form is submitted)

package_info.package_manager: custom web application (JavaScript/HTML, SaaS platform: oemapps)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is malicious because it is purpose-built to create convincing phishing websites that impersonate legitimate e-commerce brands, collect sensitive user data (credit card details, PII), and exfiltrate it to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The kit leverages dynamic language translation, abuse of legitimate payment processors, and infrastructure obfuscation to maximize effectiveness and evade detection.

attack_chain.action: Victim visits a convincing phishing site mimicking a legitimate e-commerce brand.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim interacts with the site and enters sensitive information.

attack_chain.action: Phishing site dynamically adapts language and content to match the victim's browser settings, increasing credibility and targeting both Chinese and English-speaking users.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is more likely to trust and interact with the site.

attack_chain.action: Victim enters payment or login information into fake forms presented by the phishing site.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript captures sensitive data from the DOM.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript collects and exfiltrates payment and/or login credentials to attacker-controlled infrastructure via HTTPS POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive data for financial fraud or account takeover.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript code with Mandarin comments embedded in English-facing e-commerce sites
Form data (credit card, login credentials) exfiltrated via HTTPS POST to domains unrelated to the legitimate brand
Dynamic language switching with zh-CN language tag on phishing domains
Credential or payment data collection functions that POST directly to suspicious endpoints
file_indicators: HTML documents with zh-CN language tag
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests to api.northfaceblackfriday.shop, api.lidl-blackfriday-eu.shop, and similar suspicious domains
Domains registered via West263 International Limited or Alibaba Cloud
Use of Chinese-hosted CDNs for phishing site assets
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor e-commerce sites for JavaScript containing Mandarin comments or zh-CN language tags, especially if form data is POSTed to domains not associated with the legitimate brand. Flag sites that dynamically switch language to zh-CN and exfiltrate sensitive data to suspicious endpoints. Correlate with known phishing domains and infrastructure registered through Chinese registrars or hosted on Chinese CDNs. Use behavioral signatures to identify credential or payment data collection functions that POST directly to untrusted domains.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code statically references hardcoded blockchain addresses in a JavaScript file, with no functional logic or data processing, resulting in no operational effect but potentially linking the package to blockchain-based reward systems.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Including hardcoded blockchain addresses in a file that otherwise contains no functional code is highly atypical and suggests the package may be used to game blockchain-based reward systems, act as a placeholder for future malicious payloads, or serve as a marker for automated reward collection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate npm package, especially one purporting to be an ESLint plugin, is expected to provide actual linting or utility functionality. Instead, this package is empty or contains only references to unrelated blockchain addresses, which is inconsistent with normal package development practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may include blockchain addresses for donation or configuration purposes, but not in the absence of all other meaningful functionality or code.
key_indicators: Presence of hardcoded blockchain addresses in otherwise empty or non-functional files
JavaScript files (e.g., lib/web3c.js) containing only comments or static address assignments
No functional code or exports present in the file

package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a coordinated mass-flooding campaign targeting the npm registry. It publishes hundreds of thousands of functionally useless or near-empty packages, which strains registry infrastructure, risks denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, and pollutes the open source ecosystem. The packages are interlinked via dependencies, amplifying the impact and complicating removal, and may serve as a smokescreen for more targeted malicious activity or to exploit blockchain-based reward systems.

attack_chain.action: Mass publication of thousands of packages with gibberish or auto-generated names and minimal or empty code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Floods the npm registry, straining registry resources and polluting the open source ecosystem.

attack_chain.action: Each package declares dependencies on dozens or hundreds of other similarly named packages, creating a recursive dependency web.
attack_chain.leads_to: Causes resource exhaustion during dependency resolution and complicates package removal for registry operators.

attack_chain.action: Packages reference hardcoded blockchain addresses, potentially to game blockchain-based reward systems or act as placeholders for future malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: May enable the publisher to receive crypto tokens for publishing or referencing packages, or facilitate future malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with minimal or empty code that statically reference hardcoded blockchain addresses
Packages with package.json files declaring large numbers (dozens or hundreds) of dependencies on other similarly named, functionally empty packages from the same publisher
Mass publication of packages with gibberish or auto-generated names within a short time frame, especially from a single publisher
file_indicators: lib/web3c.js containing only comments or hardcoded blockchain addresses and no functional code
package.json files with extensive dependencies on other @zitterorg/* packages that are also non-functional
network_indicators: No direct network activity in package code, but indirect indicators include spikes in npm registry access and excessive dependency resolution requests during installation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages with minimal or empty code, particularly those referencing hardcoded blockchain addresses in JavaScript files. Flag packages whose package.json declares large numbers of dependencies on other packages from the same publisher, especially when those dependencies are also functionally empty. Detect mass publication events involving gibberish or auto-generated package names from a single publisher. Registry operators should watch for sudden spikes in package publication rates and recursive dependency chains that could cause resource exhaustion or DoS conditions.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Magecart Web Skimmer (MenuDrive/Harbortouch/InTouchPOS) (N/A (Injected JavaScript on e-commerce platforms))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user submits the checkout form, the code collects the cardholder's name, email, phone number, and payment card details from the DOM, then exfiltrates this data via an HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in unauthorized theft of personal and financial information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script collects both personal and payment data from the checkout form and sends it to an external, non-legitimate endpoint (malicious-domain.com) using a fetch POST request, which is not part of the legitimate payment workflow.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should only transmit sensitive data to the payment processor or backend server of the platform, never to unknown third-party domains, and should use secure, documented APIs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate payment integrations may collect similar data, but only for processing payments with trusted providers and never transmit raw payment or PII data to untrusted domains.
key_indicators: Collection of both PII (name, email, phone) and payment data (card, exp, cvv)
Exfiltration of data to a non-standard, attacker-controlled domain (malicious-domain.com)
Use of fetch/XHR to send sensitive data externally
No user notification or consent for data transmission
Script not present in original platform codebase

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the user submits the checkout form
execution_context.file_location: Injected into MenuDrive platform checkout page as a separate script

package_info.why_malicious: The injected JavaScript code is designed to covertly collect sensitive payment card and personal information from checkout forms on restaurant ordering platforms and exfiltrate it to attacker-controlled domains. This constitutes credential theft and payment card fraud, as the data is stolen without user consent and sent to infrastructure controlled by cybercriminals.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript is injected into the checkout page of restaurant ordering platforms, either inline or as separate scripts.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious code is present and ready to execute when users interact with the checkout page.

attack_chain.action: When a user enters payment details and interacts with the checkout form (e.g., clicking the checkout button or submitting the form), the malicious script collects sensitive data from the DOM or from a fake overlay form.
attack_chain.leads_to: Collection of payment card information and personally identifiable information (PII) from users.

attack_chain.action: The collected data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains via HTTP requests (fetch/XHR) or dynamically created script tags.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives payment card and PII, enabling carding, identity theft, and fraud.

attack_chain.action: Stolen payment card data is aggregated and sold on dark web marketplaces or used directly for fraudulent transactions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Financial fraud and loss for victims, as well as reputational and regulatory impact for affected platforms.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript accessing payment form fields such as credit card number, CVV, expiration date, billing address, name, email, and phone on checkout pages
Exfiltration of form data to external domains via fetch, XMLHttpRequest, or dynamically created script tags
Creation of new form overlays or fake forms on top of legitimate checkout pages
Event handlers attached to checkout or payment buttons that trigger data exfiltration
file_indicators: Unexpected inline <script> tags or external script references on checkout pages
References to suspicious or lookalike domains (e.g., authorizen.net, malicious-domain.com) in script source URLs
Injected scripts or code blocks not present in the original platform codebase
Presence of new or modified JavaScript files (e.g., main.js) with unauthorized changes
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as authorizen.net/ord.php or malicious-domain.com/collect during checkout process
POST requests containing payment or PII data to unknown or untrusted domains
Unusual script loading activity from non-standard domains during checkout
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unexpected JavaScript accessing payment form fields and transmitting data to external domains. Scan for inline or injected scripts on checkout pages, especially those referencing suspicious or lookalike domains. Use web application firewalls (WAF) and content security policies (CSP) to block unauthorized script execution and outbound requests. Regularly audit subdomains and web assets for unauthorized code changes. Implement network monitoring to detect outbound requests to non-standard domains during checkout, and alert on POST requests containing payment or PII data to unknown endpoints.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: Single-character package name ('-')
index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_knowledge.source_package: LCBO Checkout Page Malicious Script (N/A (Web injection))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user enters payment information on the checkout page, the code collects sensitive payment data from the DOM, then transmits this data via an HTTPS POST request to an attacker-controlled external domain, resulting in real-time exfiltration of payment credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code actively harvests sensitive payment information from the checkout form and sends it to an unauthorized, external server, which is a definitive indicator of a web skimming attack.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate checkout scripts should only transmit payment data to trusted, authorized payment processors or gateways, never to unknown or unvetted external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate payment or analytics scripts may collect and transmit user data, but only to domains that are explicitly authorized and controlled by the merchant or their payment processor.
key_indicators: JavaScript code accessing and extracting payment fields from the checkout page DOM
Outbound POST requests from the checkout page to domains not associated with the merchant or payment processor
Presence of injected or modified scripts not found in the official website source code
Execution of data exfiltration logic specifically on sensitive payment entry pages

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user visits the checkout page and enters payment information
execution_context.file_location: Injected JavaScript within the LCBO checkout page HTML or a linked JavaScript file (location not present in legitimate source code repository)
required_permissions: Access to DOM elements containing payment data
Ability to initiate outbound network requests

package_info.why_malicious: The injected JavaScript code on LCBO's checkout page was specifically crafted to intercept and exfiltrate customers’ payment information in real time. This constitutes a classic web skimming (Magecart-style) attack, directly violating payment security standards and user trust by targeting sensitive financial data for theft.

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious JavaScript into the LCBO checkout page, either by compromising the website or a third-party dependency.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious skimmer code is present and ready to execute when users access the checkout page.

attack_chain.action: Injected code activates as users enter payment information, harvesting sensitive data directly from the checkout form fields.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive payment data is captured in the user's browser session.

attack_chain.action: Collected payment data is transmitted via HTTPS POST to attacker-controlled infrastructure outside the legitimate payment flow.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen payment information, achieving the objective of payment data theft.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript code on checkout or payment pages that collects values from payment input fields (e.g., credit card number, CVV, expiration date)
Outbound network requests (especially POST) from checkout pages to domains not associated with the merchant or their payment processor
Unexpected or unauthorized script modifications or injections detected on payment-related pages
file_indicators: Injected or modified JavaScript code within checkout.html, payment.js, or other files serving the checkout page
References to external scripts or domains not present in the legitimate website source code or version control
Presence of script tags or inline JavaScript that are not part of the official deployment
network_indicators: POST requests from the checkout page to domains or IP addresses not whitelisted as payment processors (e.g., attacker-controlled-domain.com)
Unusual outbound HTTPS traffic originating from payment page endpoints, especially to newly observed or untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor the integrity of JavaScript files and inline scripts on checkout/payment pages for unauthorized changes. Inspect network traffic from these pages for POST requests to domains not on an approved whitelist of payment processors. Alert on any script that collects payment data and attempts to transmit it to external, unvetted endpoints. Employ content security policies (CSP) to restrict script sources and network destinations, and regularly audit for deviations from expected script and network behaviors.
